title: Book 7 — Polymnia, Chapter 103
paragraphs: Xerxes, hearing this, laughed and said: “Demaratus, what a thing is this you have said — that a thousand men will fight with so vast an army! Come, tell me: you say that you yourself were once king of these men. Will you, then, be willing right now to fight with ten men? And yet, if your state is such throughout as you describe, you, their king, ought by your own laws to stand in battle against twice as many as another man — that is, if each one of them is a match for ten of my army, I expect you to be a match for twenty. Thus the report you give of them would be borne out. But if you, who make so great a boast, are men of the same size and quality as the Greeks I commonly deal with, yourself included, then take care that what has been said does not turn out to be an empty boast. For come, let me examine the matter by every probability. How could a thousand men, or ten thousand, or even fifty thousand, all equally free and not ruled by one man, stand against so great an army? Since, as you know, there will be more than a thousand of us for each one of them, supposing them to be five thousand in number. Now if they were ruled by one man after our fashion, they might, out of fear of him, become braver than is their nature, or they might be driven by the lash to fight with greater numbers while being fewer themselves. But left to their own freedom, they would do neither. For my part I suppose that even if they were matched equally in numbers, the Greeks would hardly dare fight the Persians alone. With us, the thing you speak of is to be found in single men — not often, but rarely; for there are some Persian spearmen of mine who will consent to fight three Greeks at a time. You have had no experience of such men, and so you speak very much at random.”
